stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Write the equation of the tangent line to the solution curve at x=0.

(b) Find d²y/dx² in terms of x and y, and use it to determine whether the solution curve is concave up or concave down at x=0.

(c) Solve the differential equation for the particular solution.

(d) Find y(1) exactly. Then use the tangent line from part (a) to approximate y(1), and state whether this approximation is an underestimate or an overestimate of y(1).
stimulus: A function y satisfies dy/dx=2x/(1+y) and y(0)=1.
canonical_answer_1: Finds the initial slope is 0 at the point (0,1). | Writes y=1. | Finds d²y/dx² = 2/(1+y) − 4x²/(1+y)³. | At (0,1), d²y/dx² = 1 > 0, so the curve is concave up at x=0. | Separates variables as (1+y)dy=2x dx. | Integrates and applies y(0)=1. | Obtains y=−1+√(2x²+4). | Finds y(1)=√6−1. | The tangent line y=1 gives 1 at x=1, an underestimate since 1 < √6−1 ≈ 1.449.

stem:
Two acetate buffers are prepared, both with a 1:1 ratio of CH3COOH to CH3COO- (pKa = 4.74), but at different total concentrations:

Buffer A: 0.10 M CH3COOH and 0.10 M CH3COO-
Buffer B: 1.0 M CH3COOH and 1.0 M CH3COO-

0.010 mol of HCl is added to 1.00 L of each buffer (assume no volume change).

(a) Calculate the initial pH of Buffer A and Buffer B. Explain why these values are the same despite the different concentrations.
(b) Without calculating a new pH, determine the amounts of CH3COOH and CH3COO- in Buffer A after the HCl is added, and use the new CH3COO-/CH3COOH ratio to predict whether the pH rises or falls.
(c) Do the same for Buffer B: determine the new amounts of CH3COOH and CH3COO-, and use the new ratio to predict whether the pH rises or falls.
(d) Based on your results in parts (b) and (c), identify which buffer has the greater buffer capacity, and explain why in terms of the amount of conjugate acid/base reserve available to react with added H+.
canonical_answer_1:
(a) Both buffers have an initial pH of 4.74. Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]); since both buffers have a 1:1 ratio of CH3COOH to CH3COO- regardless of total concentration, log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa = 4.74 for both Buffer A and Buffer B -- the total concentration does not affect pH as long as the ratio stays 1:1.
(b) Buffer A: initial mol CH3COOH = mol CH3COO- = 0.10 mol (in 1.00 L). Adding 0.010 mol HCl converts 0.010 mol CH3COO- to CH3COOH: new mol CH3COOH = 0.11 mol, new mol CH3COO- = 0.09 mol. The CH3COO-/CH3COOH ratio falls from 1.00 to 0.09/0.11, about 0.82, so the pH falls (by a noticeable amount).
(c) Buffer B: initial mol CH3COOH = mol CH3COO- = 1.0 mol. Adding 0.010 mol HCl: new mol CH3COOH = 1.01 mol, new mol CH3COO- = 0.99 mol. The ratio falls only from 1.00 to 0.99/1.01, about 0.98, so the pH falls only very slightly.
(d) Buffer B has the greater buffer capacity. Because Buffer B contains much larger absolute amounts of CH3COOH and CH3COO- (1.0 mol each versus 0.10 mol each) available to consume added H+ or OH-, the same 0.010 mol addition changes the [HA]/[A-] ratio, and therefore the pH, much less in Buffer B than in the more dilute Buffer A (ratio about 0.98 for B versus about 0.82 for A).
